title: Going places: direction and the accusative
objectives: I can say where I am with the locative and where I am going with 'у', 'в' or 'на' and the accusative.
I can tell 'де?' from 'куди́?', 'тут' from 'сюди́' and 'там' from 'туди́'.
I can choose 'іти́' for going on foot and 'ї́хати' for going by vehicle, and spell 'іти́' correctly after a vowel and after a consonant.
I can say what I can and cannot do with 'могти́' and an infinitive.
I can ask the way politely and give directions with 'пря́мо', 'ліво́руч', 'право́руч', 'споча́тку' and 'по́тім'.

vocabulary.source: to go, on foot, in one direction
vocabulary.note: Also 'йти': the form with 'й' follows a vowel. Present 'іду́', 'іде́ш', 'іду́ть', and after a vowel 'йду', 'йдеш', 'йдуть'.

example.source: Taras is walking to the park.

vocabulary.source: to go, by vehicle, in one direction
vocabulary.note: The present is built on the stem 'їд-': 'ї́ду', 'ї́деш', 'ї́дуть'. It is the verb for anyone riding in a car, a bus, a train or the metro.
Present 'мо́жу', 'мо́жеш', 'мо́жуть': the 'г' becomes 'ж' and the stress moves to the stem. An infinitive follows it.
It asks about a destination, the place someone is going to. 'Де' asks where someone or something is.
It names a direction, as 'куди́' asks for one. 'Там' names the place where something is.

example.source: The station is over there. I am going there.

vocabulary.note: It names a direction toward the speaker. 'Тут' names the place where the speaker is.
In directions it means 'straight on'. In other sentences it also means 'directly'.

vocabulary.source: on the left, to the left
vocabulary.note: It is built from 'лі́вий', left, and the root of 'рука́', hand, with 'ч' in place of 'к': on the left hand. This one word answers both 'де?' and 'куди́?'.

example.source: The pharmacy is on the left.

vocabulary.source: on the right, to the right
vocabulary.note: It is built like 'ліво́руч', from 'пра́вий', right, and the root of 'рука́', hand. It also answers both 'де?' and 'куди́?'.

example.source: The bank is on the right.

vocabulary.note: It says where something is. 'Це бли́зько?' asks whether a place is near.
It says where something is. 'Це дале́ко?' asks 'Is it far?', with 'це' pointing at the trip.
It is built from 'по', at, and the same root of 'рука́' as 'ліво́руч': at hand. It says that something is right beside you.

example.source: The café is right next door.

vocabulary.note: It orders the steps of a plan or of directions, often after 'споча́тку'.

example.target: Споча́тку я йду на по́шту, а по́тім у банк.
example.source: First I am going to the post office, and then to the bank.

vocabulary.note: It is built from 'з', from, and the noun 'поча́ток', beginning, so it says 'from the beginning'. It opens the first step.
It is regular, like 'чита́ти': 'поверта́ю', 'поверта́єш'. With 'ліво́руч' or 'право́руч' it gives directions.
It is built from 'пере-', across, and 'хрест', cross: a place where roads cross. Locative 'на перехре́сті'.

example.source: There is a traffic light at the intersection.

vocabulary.note: It is built from 'сві́тло', light, and '-фор', a Greek root meaning 'carrier'. Locative 'на світлофо́рі'.

example.source: We are standing at the traffic light.

vocabulary.note: A means of transport takes 'на' and the locative: 'на авто́бусі', by bus.

example.source: Where is the bus to the station?

vocabulary.note: It never changes form, like 'кафе́': 'на метро́', 'у метро́'.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: 'іти́' and 'йти', 'ї́хати', 'могти́' and the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every new word of this unit is read with the rules of units 1 to 4. A few of them show those rules at work in ways worth looking at closely, and one, 'могти́', has a sound change that the spelling does not show.

'Іти́' and 'йти' are one verb with two spellings, and the choice follows the same euphony rule as 'і' and 'й' in unit 4. Euphony means choosing the form that is easiest to say in its place: Ukrainian avoids two vowels meeting across words and long runs of consonants. After a vowel the verb begins with 'й'; after a consonant it begins with 'і':

- 'Я йду.', 'Вона́ йде.', 'Ми йдемо́.' (after a vowel)
- 'Він іде́.', 'Тара́с іде́.', 'Сем іде́.' (after a consonant)
- 'Я мо́жу йти.' but 'Ти мо́жеш іти́.' (the same rule for the infinitive)

The 'й' at the start of 'йду' is the [j] of 'чай'. Like the 'й' meaning 'and' in unit 4, it makes no syllable of its own and joins the vowel before it, so 'я йду' sounds like [jɑj du]. Because 'й' is not a vowel, 'йду', 'йдеш', 'йде' and 'йдуть' each have one vowel, so they are one-syllable words and carry no stress mark, while 'іду́', with two vowels, does.

'Ї́хати' begins with 'ї', which is always [ji], so the word starts like English 'yee': [ˈjixɑtɪ]. Its present has 'д' where the infinitive has 'ха' ('ї́ду', 'ї́деш'), and the stress stays on the 'ї' in every form. The present of 'ї́сти', to eat, also begins with 'ї' ('їм', 'їдя́ть'): 'ї́ду' is 'I am going', 'їдя́ть' is 'they eat'.

'Могти́' is said [mɔxˈtɪ]. Unit 2 showed that Ukrainian keeps a voiced consonant voiced at the end of a word and before most other consonants, and that 'г' before 'к' or 'т' is the exception, as in 'ле́гко': it loses its voice and is said [x], the sound of 'х' in 'хліб'. In the present the 'г' is replaced by 'ж' in every form ('мо́жу', 'мо́жеш', 'мо́жуть'), and the stress moves from the ending of the infinitive to the stem.

The other new words apply the rules directly:

- 'бли́зько' keeps its 'з' voiced before 'к', and the soft sign makes it soft: [ˈblɪzʲkɔ]
- 'авто́бус' has 'в' at the end of a syllable, said [w] as in 'Петрі́вна': [ɑwˈtɔbus]
- 'сюди́' and 'пря́мо' have a consonant softened by 'ю' or 'я'; 'р' is soft before 'я'
- 'куди́', 'туди́' and 'сюди́' have a hard 'д' before 'и'
- 'по́тім' and 'ліво́руч' have a consonant softened by 'і'

'Перехре́стя' is a neuter noun in '-я'. Unit 5 showed such nouns with a doubled consonant before the ending ('життя́', 'ре́чення'), but the consonant doubles only when a single consonant stands between the vowel and '-я'. In 'перехре́стя' two consonants, 'с' and 'т', stand there, so nothing is doubled. Without the doubled letter the ending does not show the gender, since 'пі́сня', song, also has two consonants before '-я' and is feminine, so 'перехре́стя' is learned as a neuter noun. 'Я' softens the 'т', and the 'с' before it becomes soft too: [pɛrɛˈxrɛsʲtʲɑ]. In the locative 'на перехре́сті' the ending '-і' keeps both soft.

'Споча́тку' is built from 'з', from, and 'поча́тку', a form of 'поча́ток', beginning, which drops the 'о' of its last syllable as 'ри́нок' does in other forms. Unit 4 showed that 'з' sounds close to [s] before a voiceless consonant such as 'п'. When it becomes part of a word, before 'к', 'п', 'т', 'ф' or 'х', it is also written 'с'.

'Світлофо́р' joins 'сві́тло', light, and '-фор'. Every consonant of 'тл' is said, and the stress falls on the last syllable, on the part '-фор'. 'Метро́', like 'кафе́' and 'меню́', is a borrowed noun that never changes form.

examples.source: Oksana is going, and Taras is going too.
You can walk slowly.
They are going by bus.
The metro is close, and the intersection is far.

grammar.title: Where and where to: 'де?' with the locative, 'куди́?' with the accusative
grammar.explanation:
English uses 'where' both for 'Where is she?' and for 'Where is she going?', and it changes the preposition: 'in the park' against 'to the park'. Ukrainian does the opposite. It keeps the same preposition, 'у' (or 'в') or 'на', and changes the case of the noun after it. Each case answers its own question:

- the locative (unit 12) says where someone or something is, and answers 'де?', where
- the accusative (unit 10) says where someone or something is going, and answers 'куди́?', where to

So 'у па́рку' is 'in the park' and 'у парк' is 'to the park'; 'на по́шті' is 'at the post office' and 'на по́шту' is 'to the post office'. The accusative fits this job because it is the case of the goal of an action. In 'Я ба́чу парк' the park is what the seeing reaches; in 'Я йду в парк' it is what the going reaches.

The endings are the accusative endings of unit 10:

- feminine nouns in '-а' take '-у' and nouns in '-я' take '-ю': 'на по́шту', 'на ву́лицю', 'на ку́хню'
- masculine nouns for things do not change: 'у парк', 'на вокза́л', 'у Ки́їв'
- neuter nouns do not change: 'у мі́сто'; 'кафе́' and 'метро́' never change at all
- 'ва́нна', bathroom, declines like an adjective, and the feminine adjective ending is also '-у': 'у ва́нну'
- an adjective takes the accusative too: 'у вели́ку кімна́ту', 'у вели́кий парк', 'у вели́ке мі́сто'

A place takes the same preposition for both questions. If a place is 'на по́шті' when you are there, you go 'на по́шту'; if it is 'у шко́лі', you go 'у шко́лу'. Cities and countries take 'у': 'у Львів', 'в Украї́ну'. The choice between 'у' and 'в' follows the euphony rule of unit 4 in both cases.

The verb usually tells you which question the sentence answers. Verbs of being somewhere, such as 'жи́ти', 'працюва́ти', 'сиді́ти' and 'стоя́ти', take the locative. Verbs of moving, such as 'іти́' and 'ї́хати', take the accusative. One sentence can hold both: 'Я живу́ в Ки́єві, а за́втра ї́ду у Львів.'

Ukrainian makes the same split in its adverbs of place, where English uses one word for both:

- 'де?', where, and 'куди́?', where to
- 'тут', here, and 'сюди́', here, to this place
- 'там', there, and 'туди́', there, to that place
- 'вдо́ма', at home, and 'додо́му', home, toward home

A few adverbs serve both questions: 'ліво́руч' and 'право́руч' say where something is ('Апте́ка ліво́руч.') and where someone turns ('Ви поверта́єте ліво́руч.').

examples.source: I am in the park.
I am going to the park.
She is at the post office.
She is going to the post office.

examples.target: Я живу́ в Ки́єві, а за́втра ї́ду у Львів.
examples.source: I live in Kyiv, and tomorrow I am going to Lviv.
examples.source_literal: I live in Kyiv, and tomorrow I-ride to Lviv.

examples.target: Ми вдо́ма, а Сем іде́ додо́му.
examples.source: We are at home, and Sam is walking home.
examples.source_literal: we at-home, and Sam goes homeward.

grammar.title: On foot or by vehicle: 'іти́' and 'ї́хати'
grammar.explanation:
The English verb 'go' does not say how you travel. Ukrainian has to say it, because it has no neutral verb for a trip under way:

- 'іти́' when the person moves on foot
- 'ї́хати' when the person rides in or on a vehicle: a car, a bus, a train, the metro, a bicycle

So a trip from Kyiv to Lviv is always 'Я ї́ду у Львів.', and a walk to the shop on the corner is 'Я йду в магази́н.' When you do not know how someone travels, ask: 'Ти йдеш чи ї́деш?', are you walking or riding?

Both verbs describe movement in one direction, toward one goal. Their present covers a trip under way now ('Я йду на по́шту.', I am walking to the post office) and, with a time word, a trip planned for soon ('За́втра я ї́ду у Львів.'), just as English 'I am going' does. They are not used for a regular habit, such as going to school every day, or for a trip there and back; A2 teaches a second pair of verbs for those.

Both verbs belong to the first conjugation (endings '-у', '-еш', '-е', '-емо', '-ете', '-уть'), but neither shows its present stem in the infinitive: 'іти́' has the stem 'ід-' and 'ї́хати' the stem 'їд-'. The stress of 'іти́' stays on the ending in every form ('іду́', 'іде́ш', 'ідемо́'), and the stress of 'ї́хати' stays on 'ї' ('ї́ду', 'ї́демо'). After a vowel, the forms of 'іти́' begin with 'й' instead of 'і', as the spelling note explains. Most subject pronouns end in a vowel, so after them the forms with 'й' are the usual ones ('я йду', 'ти йдеш', 'вони́ йдуть'); after 'він' and after a name ending in a consonant it is 'іде́'.

The means of transport takes 'на' and the locative, as English says 'on the bus': 'на авто́бусі', by bus; 'на метро́', by metro. The accusative after 'на' names a goal instead: 'Я йду на зупи́нку.' is 'I am walking to the bus stop'.

When the vehicle itself is the subject, Ukrainian often says 'іде́': 'Авто́бус іде́ в центр.', the bus goes downtown. With 'сюди́', 'іти́' says that someone is coming toward the speaker: 'Окса́на йде сюди́.', Oksana is coming here.

examples.source: Are you walking or taking transport?
Sam is walking to the library.
Tomorrow Oksana is going to Canada.

examples.target: Я ї́ду на авто́бусі в центр.
examples.source: I am taking the bus downtown.
examples.source_literal: I ride on bus to center.

examples.source: The bus goes downtown.

grammar.title: 'Могти́' with an infinitive, and directions in the present
grammar.explanation:
'Могти́' means 'to be able', and it is the Ukrainian 'can'. Like English 'can', it is followed directly by an infinitive, with no word for 'to' between them: 'Я мо́жу ї́хати.', I can go. Unlike English 'can', it is an ordinary verb that changes for every person. It belongs to the first conjugation, its 'г' becomes 'ж' in every present form, and its stress sits on the stem: 'мо́жу', 'мо́жеш', 'мо́же'. 'Не' goes before it, as before any verb: 'Я не мо́жу йти.', I can't go. The infinitive after it follows euphony: 'мо́жу йти' after a vowel, 'мо́жеш іти́' after a consonant.

A question with 'могти́' is also a polite request, as in English: 'Ви мо́жете говори́ти пові́льно?', can you speak slowly? 'Могти́' is different from 'мо́жна' (unit 10). 'Мо́жна' is a predicative word, the whole predicate of a sentence with no grammatical subject, so it names nobody: 'Мо́жна ка́ву?', literally 'possible coffee?', asks whether coffee may be had. 'Могти́' is a verb with a subject, the person who is able: 'Я мо́жу пи́ти ка́ву.', I can drink coffee.

Directions can be given in the present tense, addressed to 'ви' or, between friends, to 'ти'. English does the same when it says 'You go straight, then you turn left'. Ukrainian can also give directions in the imperative, the mood of commands that unit 6 named ('чита́й', read), whose forms A2 teaches. The present is natural and polite:

- 'Ви йдете́ пря́мо.', you go straight ahead
- 'По́тім ви поверта́єте ліво́руч.', then you turn left
- 'На перехре́сті ви поверта́єте право́руч.', at the intersection you turn right

The steps are ordered with 'споча́тку', first, and 'по́тім', then. A landmark where you turn is in the locative after 'на': 'на перехре́сті', 'на світлофо́рі', 'на пло́щі'. A goal you walk toward is in the accusative: 'Ви йдете́ на пло́щу.' 'Бли́зько', 'дале́ко' and 'по́руч' say how far a place is: 'Апте́ка по́руч.'

To ask the way, begin with 'Ви́бачте' and ask with 'де': 'Ви́бачте, де вокза́л?' Then 'Це дале́ко?' asks whether it is far, with 'це' pointing at the trip.

examples.source: Can you speak Ukrainian?
I can't go tomorrow.

examples.target: Споча́тку ви йдете́ пря́мо, по́тім поверта́єте право́руч.
examples.source: First you go straight ahead, then you turn right.
At the traffic light you turn left.
Excuse me, where is the pharmacy? Is it far?

culture.title: Getting around a Ukrainian city
culture.text:
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipro have a metro, and in Kyiv it is the fastest way to cross the city. The Kyiv metro opened in 1960. Its station 'Арсена́льна' is one of the deepest in the world, about 105 meters below the street, and the ride down on its escalators takes several minutes.

Buses, trams and trolleybuses cover the rest of a city, together with minibuses that run a fixed route. A minibus of this kind is called 'маршру́тка', from 'маршру́т', route. It stops where passengers ask, so a rider tells the driver where to stop.

To ask the way, Ukrainians open with 'Ви́бачте' and use 'ви' with a stranger. Directions are usually given by landmarks rather than street names: a pharmacy, a square, a metro station, a traffic light. Pedestrians cross at a traffic light or a marked crossing, and crossing elsewhere can be fined.

The main street of Kyiv is 'Хреща́тик'. Its name shares a root with 'хрест', cross, the same root as in 'перехре́стя'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Which question asks where someone is going?
choices: Де ти?
Куди́ ти йдеш?
Хто там?
Як спра́ви?
exercises.explanation: 'Куди́' asks for a destination, the place someone is going to. 'Де ти?' asks where someone is.

choices: I am at the pharmacy.
I am going to the bank.
I am going to the pharmacy.

exercises.prompt: Olena is taking the metro downtown. What does she say?
choices: Я йду в центр.
Я в це́нтрі.
Я ї́ду в центр.
exercises.explanation: Riding the metro is going by vehicle, so the verb is 'ї́хати', and the goal 'в центр' is in the accusative. 'Я йду' would mean she is walking, and 'в це́нтрі' says where she is.

exercises.hint_source: Taras is going to the post office.
exercises.explanation: A goal after 'на' is in the accusative, and a feminine noun in '-а' takes '-у': 'по́шта' becomes 'по́шту'.
Where someone is takes the locative. 'Бібліоте́ка' takes '-і', and the 'к' before it becomes 'ц'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'па́рку' in 'Я в па́рку' but 'парк' in 'Я йду в парк'?
choices: Both mean the same, and either can be used.
'Па́рку' is the locative, for where someone is; 'парк' is the accusative, for where someone is going.
'Парк' is the form used after a vowel.
'Па́рку' is a plural form.
exercises.explanation: The preposition stays the same and the case changes. The locative answers 'де?', and the accusative answers 'куди́?'. A masculine noun for a thing does not change in the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its meaning

choices: Where are you going?
Are you walking or taking transport?
Are you at home or at work?

exercises.explanation: Movement toward the speaker answers 'куди́?', so the word is 'сюди́'. 'Тут' says where someone is.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'Вона́ йде' but 'Він іде́'?
choices: 'Йде' is the feminine form of the verb.
'Іде́' is used only for men.
After a vowel the verb begins with 'й', and after a consonant with 'і'.
'Йде' is used for going by vehicle.
exercises.explanation: This is euphony, the rule of unit 4 for 'і' and 'й'. 'Вона́' ends in a vowel, so 'йде' follows; 'він' ends in a consonant, so 'іде́' follows. The present tense does not change for gender.
Riding a bus takes 'ї́хати', and the form for 'ми' is 'ї́демо', on the stem 'їд-'.

exercises.hint_source: Sam is going to the university.
exercises.explanation: A goal is in the accusative, and a masculine noun for a thing keeps its dictionary form.

exercises.prompt: 'Ї́ду' and 'їдя́ть' both begin with 'ї'. What do they mean?
choices: 'I am going by vehicle' and 'they eat'
'I eat' and 'they are going by vehicle'
Both are forms of 'ї́сти', to eat
Both are forms of 'ї́хати', to go by vehicle
exercises.explanation: 'Ї́ду' is the form of 'ї́хати' for 'я', on the stem 'їд-'. 'Їдя́ть' is the form of 'ї́сти', to eat, for 'вони́'.
'Могти́' has 'ж' in every present form, and the form for 'я' is 'мо́жу'. The infinitive 'йти' follows it directly.

choices: The bank is right nearby, on the right.
The pharmacy is far away, on the left.
The pharmacy is right nearby, on the right.

exercises.prompt_source: I am walking to the post office.

exercises.hint_source: They are going to Lviv by train.
exercises.explanation: A train is a vehicle, so the verb is 'ї́хати', and the form for 'вони́' is 'ї́дуть'.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Мо́жна ка́ву?' and 'Я мо́жу пи́ти ка́ву.'?
choices: 'Мо́жна' is a predicative word in a sentence with no subject; 'мо́жу' is a form of the verb 'могти́', with 'я' as its subject.
'Мо́жна' is the form of 'могти́' for 'ви'.
There is no difference in structure.
'Мо́жу' is used only in questions.
exercises.explanation: 'Мо́жна' names nobody: it asks whether coffee may be had. 'Могти́' is a verb with a subject, the person who is able, and it changes for every person.

choices: [ɦ], as everywhere else
[x], like the 'х' of 'хліб', because it stands before 'т'
[g], like 'ґ'
It is silent
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian keeps voiced consonants voiced, with one main exception: 'г' before 'к' or 'т' is said [x]. In the present the 'г' is replaced by 'ж': 'мо́жу'.

exercises.prompt_source: Tomorrow I am going to Lviv.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'перехре́стя' have no doubled consonant before '-я', while 'життя́' doubles its 'т'?
choices: 'Перехре́стя' is a feminine noun.
The stress falls on the ending in 'життя́'.
The letter 'с' is never doubled.
Two consonants, 'с' and 'т', stand before '-я', and only a single consonant is doubled in such nouns.
exercises.explanation: A neuter noun in '-я' doubles the consonant before the ending only when one consonant stands between the vowel and '-я', as in 'життя́'. In 'перехре́стя' the 'с' and the 'т' stand there, so nothing doubles.

exercises.prompt_source: Taras is taking the bus to the market.
She is walking to the park.
exercises.explanation: Walking takes 'іти́', and after the vowel of 'вона́' it is 'йде'. A goal takes the accusative, and 'парк' does not change.

exercises.prompt_source: The bank is on the right, and the café is on the left.
exercises.explanation: 'Ліво́руч' says where something is as well as which way someone turns, and the sentence needs no word for 'is'.

exercises.prompt_source: First you go straight ahead, then you turn left.
Excuse me, is the railway station far?
exercises.explanation: 'Ви́бачте' opens a question to a stranger. 'Дале́ко' is the whole predicate, with no word for 'is', and 'чи' may open the question.

exercises.prompt_source: I live in Kyiv, but I am going to Lviv.
answers: Я живу́ в Ки́єві, але́ ї́ду у Львів.
Я живу́ в Ки́єві, але́ я ї́ду у Львів.
Живу́ в Ки́єві, але́ ї́ду у Львів.
Живу́ в Ки́єві, але́ я ї́ду у Львів.
Я живу́ в Ки́єві, а ї́ду у Львів.
Я живу́ в Ки́єві, а я ї́ду у Львів.
Живу́ в Ки́єві, а ї́ду у Львів.
Живу́ в Ки́єві, а я ї́ду у Львів.
exercises.explanation: Living somewhere takes the locative, 'в Ки́єві'; going somewhere takes the accusative, 'у Львів'. A trip to another city is by vehicle, so the verb is 'ї́хати'.

exercises.hint_source: The station is far, but the metro is close.
